title: Blood component transfusion
blurb: Give blood components safely: identify the patient, time the observations, spot a reaction early and act on it.
question: Twenty minutes into a unit of red cells, Mrs Adeyemi's temperature has risen from 36.8°C to 38.9°C and she is shivering. Her blood pressure has fallen. What should the nurse do first?

teach.body: A blood component (red cells, platelets or plasma) is a living product matched to one patient. SHOT, the UK haemovigilance scheme, has repeatedly found that patients are harmed, and some die, after receiving the wrong blood. So the BSH guideline builds administration on three principles: patient identification, documentation and communication. In plain terms: prove who the patient is at every step, write everything down, and tell people what is happening.
teach.cite: BSH, The administration of blood components (2017); SHOT

teach.body: At sampling, collection and the bedside, the patient is identified positively: ask them to state their full name and date of birth where they can, and match this exactly with the identity band and the compatibility label on the component. SHOT recommends a structured bedside checklist. If anything does not match, do not start; contact the transfusion laboratory. NICE NG24 also suggests considering electronic patient identification systems.

teach.h: Suspected reaction: what to do first
items: Stop the transfusion temporarily but keep the venous access open.
Assess airway, breathing and circulation; call a doctor at once if the reaction looks severe or life-threatening.
Recheck identity: patient, identity band and the compatibility label on the component.
Look at the bag for clumps, discolouration or anything unusual; take a full set of observations.
Keep the bag and giving set: implicated units go back to the laboratory if a moderate or severe reaction is investigated.

teach.h: Mild, moderate or severe? (febrile and allergic)
teach.caption: Classification adapted from SHOT/ISBT. Anaphylaxis is treated with IM adrenaline. Moderate fever raises the possibility of bacterial contamination or haemolysis.

teach.body: Transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO) is acute or worsening breathlessness or pulmonary oedema during or up to 12 hours after transfusion, with signs of fluid overload. SHOT's pre-transfusion risk assessment asks about heart failure, regular diuretics, severe anaemia, pulmonary oedema, positive fluid balance, recent IV fluids, peripheral oedema, low albumin and significant renal impairment. If risks exist: review the need, dose carefully (often a single unit), measure fluid balance, consider a prophylactic diuretic and monitor closely.

teach.h: Scenario: Mrs Adeyemi on the haematology ward
teach.body: Nurse Priya starts a unit of red cells for Mrs Adeyemi, 64. At 20 minutes her temperature is 38.9°C (from 36.8°C), she has rigors and her BP has dropped. This is not a mild reaction. Priya stops the transfusion, keeps the cannula patent, calls the doctor urgently, assesses ABCDE and rechecks the band against the label. The bag and giving set are kept for the laboratory. The reaction is documented and reported through the hospital transfusion team.

teach.text: Don't confuse 'stop and keep the line open' with 'remove the cannula'. Venous access is kept for treatment. And don't confuse a mild fever (a 1–2°C rise to 38°C or more, nothing else) where the transfusion may continue under direct observation with a moderate one (rise of 2°C or more, 39°C or more, or rigors), which needs the transfusion stopped and urgent review.

items: Positive patient identification at every step: patient, band and compatibility label must match.
Obs: baseline within 60 min before; pulse, BP and temperature at 15 min; again within 60 min after the unit.
Red cells completed within 4 hours of leaving storage.
NICE NG24: threshold 70 g/L (80 g/L in ACS); single unit then reassess in non-bleeding adults.
Reaction: stop, keep access, ABC, check identity, call doctor; keep the bag; report moderate and severe reactions.
Tell patients the reason, risks and alternatives, and that they can no longer donate blood.

summary: You can now carry out the identity and observation steps of a safe transfusion and apply NICE NG24 thresholds. You can also grade an acute reaction, act on it in the right order and recognise patients at risk of TACO.

A.q: Before a unit of red cells is hung, the nurse is completing the bedside check for Mr Lewis, who is alert. Which action best achieves positive patient identification?
options: Reading his name from the bed board to the second checker
Confirming his hospital number with the nurse in charge
Checking the compatibility label against the prescription chart
Asking his name and DOB, then matching band and label
A.why: Positive identification means the patient states their own details where able, and these are matched exactly with the identity band and the compatibility label on the component (BSH 2017).

whyNot.0: Bed boards are not a reliable identifier; patients move beds and boards are wrong.
whyNot.1: Another nurse's confirmation is not identification of the patient in front of you.
whyNot.2: Checking the label against the chart is part of the check, but it does not prove the person in the bed is that patient.

A.q: A unit of red cells starts at 14:00. By what point should the nurse next record pulse, blood pressure and temperature?
A.why: BSH: pulse, blood pressure and temperature 15 minutes after the start of each unit, because serious reactions often begin early.

whyNot.0: Five minutes is not the standard timepoint; the BSH timepoint is 15 minutes.
whyNot.2: Thirty minutes is too late for the first check; early reactions could be missed.
whyNot.3: An hour is too long without observations after starting a unit.

A.q: A unit of red cells left the blood fridge at 09:30. By what time should the transfusion be completed?
A.why: Red cells should be completed within 4 hours of leaving temperature-controlled storage (BSH), so by 13:30.

whyNot.0: Two hours is shorter than required and may cause a rushed rate in someone at risk of overload.
whyNot.1: Three hours is within the limit, but the limit itself is 4 hours, so 13:30 is the correct deadline.
whyNot.3: Five hours exceeds the limit and increases the risk of bacterial growth in the unit.

B.q: Forty minutes into a red cell transfusion, Mr Patel, 58, develops an itchy rash on his arms. His observations are unchanged and he has no other symptoms. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Stop it permanently, remove the cannula and return the unit to the lab
Give IM adrenaline and put out a cardiac arrest call
Pause, check identity, inform the doctor, then continue observed
Increase the rate so the unit finishes before it worsens
B.why: An isolated rash or itch is a mild allergic reaction. The transfusion is paused and checks are made; it may then continue with appropriate treatment (such as an antihistamine) and direct observation (BSH ATR guidance).

whyNot.0: Removing venous access is wrong in any reaction, and a mild skin reaction does not require the unit to be abandoned.
whyNot.1: IM adrenaline is for anaphylaxis; Mr Patel has no airway, breathing or circulation problem.
whyNot.3: Speeding up a transfusion during a reaction increases exposure and the risk of overload.

B.q: Gladys, 86, has heart failure, takes furosemide daily and has ankle oedema. She is prescribed two units of red cells for anaemia without bleeding. Which risk should the nurse raise before starting?
options: Transfusion-associated circulatory overload
Febrile non-haemolytic transfusion reaction
Delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction (DHTR)
Iron overload from regular transfusion
B.why: Heart failure, a regular diuretic and peripheral oedema are all items on the SHOT TACO pre-transfusion risk assessment. NICE NG24 suggests single-unit transfusion and reassessment in adults without active bleeding.

whyNot.1: Febrile reactions are linked to the unit itself, not to heart failure or oedema.
whyNot.2: Delayed haemolysis relates to red cell antibodies, which nothing in her history suggests.
whyNot.3: Iron overload is a concern with long-term chronic transfusion, not a single episode.

B.q: Which information does NICE NG24 say should be given to a person who has had a blood transfusion?
options: That they should wait a year before donating blood
That they can no longer donate blood
That they must carry a transfusion alert card
That they need a blood test a week later
B.why: NICE NG24 rec 1.14.2 and 1.14.4: explain the reason, risks and benefits, the process, alternatives, and that they are no longer eligible to donate blood; this also goes on the discharge summary to the GP.

whyNot.0: There is no waiting period; NICE says people who have been transfused are no longer eligible to donate.
whyNot.2: Alert cards are used for some specific needs, such as antibodies, but are not a general NG24 requirement.
whyNot.3: Follow-up bloods depend on the clinical situation; a routine one-week test is not an NG24 recommendation.

C.q: Fifteen minutes into a unit of red cells, Mr Novak, 70, becomes restless and says his back hurts. His temperature is 39.2°C, pulse 124 and BP 88/50. What is the nurse's first action?
options: Give paracetamol and recheck observations in 15 minutes
Slow the transfusion rate and give an antihistamine
Stop the transfusion, keep the line open and get urgent help
Finish the unit quickly, then send a sample to the laboratory
C.why: Fever of 39°C or more with hypotension, tachycardia and pain suggests a severe reaction such as acute haemolysis or bacterial contamination. Stop the transfusion, maintain venous access, assess ABC and call a doctor immediately, then recheck identity (BSH ATR guidance).

whyNot.0: Paracetamol alone suits an isolated mild febrile reaction, not one with shock.
whyNot.1: Slowing and an antihistamine are for mild allergic reactions; continuing exposes him to more of a possibly incompatible unit.
whyNot.3: Continuing a unit that may be causing a haemolytic reaction risks death; it must be stopped.

C.q: After stopping a transfusion because of a moderate reaction, what should the nurse do with the blood bag and giving set?
options: Dispose of both in the orange clinical waste bag
Keep them for return to the transfusion laboratory
Flush the giving set and reuse it for saline
Send the bag to the pharmacy department for destruction
C.why: Implicated units should be returned to the laboratory for investigation, for example culture and repeat compatibility, and so the blood service can withdraw linked components (BSH ATR guidance).

whyNot.0: Discarding them destroys evidence needed to find the cause.
whyNot.2: The set may contain the implicated component; keep venous access with a new line and fluid, and keep the set for the lab.
whyNot.3: Blood components are traced through the transfusion laboratory, not pharmacy.

C.q: An hour after her second unit, Rose, 79, becomes breathless with crackles at both lung bases, SpO2 89% and BP 172/96. Her fluid balance is 2 litres positive. What is the most likely cause?
options: Febrile non-haemolytic transfusion reaction
Moderate allergic transfusion reaction
Hypotensive transfusion reaction
Transfusion-associated circulatory overload
C.why: New breathlessness with signs of pulmonary oedema, hypertension and a positive fluid balance within 12 hours of transfusion fits TACO (SHOT definition). She needs urgent medical review.

whyNot.0: A febrile reaction causes fever and rigors, not pulmonary oedema with a high BP.
whyNot.1: Allergic reactions cause urticaria, wheeze or angioedema, not crackles with hypertension and a positive fluid balance.
whyNot.2: A hypotensive reaction is a fall in systolic BP, whereas Rose is hypertensive.

reteach.title: Match, watch, act
reteach.question: If you remember only three words for transfusion, what should they be?

blocks.body: MATCH: the patient's own stated name and date of birth, the identity band and the compatibility label must agree before you start. WATCH: baseline observations, a full check at 15 minutes, direct observation throughout and observations after the unit. ACT: any new symptom means stop, keep the line, check ABC and identity, and get help in proportion to severity.

blocks.text: The 4-hour limit runs from when red cells leave temperature-controlled storage, not from when you hang the bag.

explain.body: Positive patient identification at sampling, collection and bedside. The patient states name and date of birth where able; these match the band and the compatibility label. Any discrepancy: do not transfuse.

test.q: At the bedside check, the date of birth on the compatibility label differs by one day from the patient's identity band. What should the nurse do?
options: Start the unit, as the name and hospital number match
Correct the label by hand and initial it
Ask the patient which date is correct and proceed
Not start it and contact the transfusion laboratory
test.why: Any discrepancy means the unit must not be given; the laboratory must resolve it (BSH 2017).

whyNot.0: A partial match is not a match; wrong-blood incidents happen through small discrepancies.
whyNot.1: Labels must never be altered at the bedside.
whyNot.2: The patient's answer does not fix a labelling error on the component.

explain.body: Baseline pulse, BP, temperature and respiratory rate within 60 minutes before. Pulse, BP and temperature at 15 minutes after starting each unit. Repeat within 60 minutes after the unit ends. Observe directly throughout.

test.q: Baseline observations for a transfusion should be taken no more than how long before the unit starts?
options: 15 minutes
30 minutes
60 minutes
4 hours
test.why: BSH: baseline observations no more than 60 minutes before the start.

whyNot.0: 15 minutes is the first check after starting.
whyNot.1: 30 minutes is not the BSH limit; it is 60.
whyNot.3: 4 hours is the completion limit for red cells, not the baseline window.

explain.body: Mild: temperature 38°C or more with a 1–2°C rise and nothing else, or itch or rash alone: may continue with treatment and direct observation. Moderate: 39°C or more, rise of 2°C or more, rigors, wheeze or angioedema. Severe: shock, bronchospasm, stridor, anaphylaxis.

bands.label: with shock or urgent review needed

test.q: During a transfusion, a patient's temperature rises from 37.0°C to 38.2°C. He feels well and other observations are unchanged. How is this best classified?
options: Mild febrile reaction
Moderate febrile reaction
Severe febrile reaction
Transfusion-associated circulatory overload
test.why: 38°C or more with a rise of 1–2°C and no other symptoms is mild (SHOT/BSH classification).

whyNot.1: Moderate needs 39°C or more, a rise of 2°C or more, or rigors and other symptoms.
whyNot.2: Severe involves serious symptoms needing urgent intervention.
whyNot.3: TACO is respiratory compromise and fluid overload, not isolated fever.

explain.body: NICE NG24: restrictive threshold 70 g/L (target 70–90 g/L); 80 g/L in acute coronary syndrome (target 80–100 g/L); individual thresholds for chronic transfusion-dependent anaemia. Single unit then reassess in adults without active bleeding.

test.q: Under NICE NG24, what red cell transfusion threshold should be considered for a patient with acute coronary syndrome?
options: 70 g/L
80 g/L
90 g/L
test.why: NICE NG24 rec 1.5.3: threshold 80 g/L with a target of 80–100 g/L in acute coronary syndrome.

whyNot.0: 70 g/L is the restrictive threshold for most adults without ACS.
whyNot.2: 90 g/L is the upper end of the standard post-transfusion target.
whyNot.3: 100 g/L is the upper end of the ACS target, not the threshold.
